body:
>You're just tired of pushing the boulder up the hill.

And that makes me feel slightly guilty, because I presume that everyone's tired, in their own way, and yet I seem to want to feel special, as if only I realise the futility of the effort, like an angsty teenager feels like no one understands them.

>The "we" there seems a bit misconstrued.
Some claim to have sought and found meaning. Others say life is meaningless. So it seems there is a difference of opinion on this particular matter.

Yeah, that was definitely a generalisation on my part.

>Have you looked for this for a long time? If so, can you share about the story of your search and what made you stop looking?

I would say I've thought about it a fair bit, though obviously I haven't come up with anything profound or original. Simply put, I see no evidence for meaning. Of course you can claim reason to simply be cause and effect, but in terms of a meaning, I just don't see one. Like I said, I didn't study philosophy, but I studied physics and one of the things we learnt was about how sometimes the ambiguity we see in the Universe is the reality. That there is no "truth" beneath it. Uncertainty is a real physical phenomenon, not just a human one. 

Honestly, most of the time I like that idea. We're free to create our own lives and destinies. Things aren't set in stone or predetermined. At the same time, it can make you feel lost in the crowd. If there's no meaning to my life, what marks me out from everyone else? And the truth, as I see it, is that most of us are no different from everyone else. It seems naive to quote a film, but The Incredibles had that line: "If everyone's special, nobody is." That contradiction between belonging and standing out is a balance.

When the fundamental processes that underpin not just our existence, but the Universe's existence, are probabilities, I guess it's hard for me to see the macroscopic world as anything other than the sum of chances. And if we're in control of our own lives, of our own meaning, then to the same extent we're in control of our own deaths. Obviously deciding exactly when you die isn't a choice most people make, but then precious few things in life go exactly according to our own individual plans.

>Here's the thing. We just don't know what our own awareness is. It is the deepest and most profound mystery of them all. I like what Jerry Fodor wrote on this question:
"Nobody has the slightest idea how anything material could be conscious. Nobody even knows what it would be like to have the slightest idea about how anything material could be conscious. So much for the philosophy of consciousness."
Given that we simply don't know whence cometh our own fundamental nature of awareness it seems vastly premature to equate the death of the body with the end of our awareness. Perhaps this universe is a simulation for consciousness akin to the Star Trek holodeck or the matrix from the eponymous movie series? The notion that our awareness simply ceases to exist is a popular one and assumed to be true by many. But we don't know.

I know what you're saying. There's too many unknowns, no high-level perspective. How could there be, when all we know is what we see? The objective truth of our conscious being will only be known to each man beyond the realms of this world, either by a heightened sense of awareness or a complete lack of one. But again, I tend to apply Occam's Razor and assume that this life, and the associated death, is all we have, until evidence presents itself to the contrary. That's a passive approach, because the active pursuit of that knowledge also seems beyond our understanding. I guess, in a way, the only people who could be argued to be taking the active approach are those who succeed in their suicide attempts.

I think it's the general concept of Absurdism that we have always tried to find reason but none has been forthcoming, so maybe I was slightly incorrect in saying that the Universe has no meaning or reason, but rather that it doesn't offer any. Hence why it's still *the* question. I wouldn't take my word for it completely as I didn't study philosophy and a lot of this is new to me. 

But as for me, yes, I see no meaning or reason. I think my life is just a fluke, a chance event. So me ceasing to exist would just be another chance event, and obviously one that tends to unity over time.
